inserts.title: Waggle angles vary across repeated runs
paragraphs: The absolute flight bearing also depends on the sun's current position, not on the comb angle alone. Because the sun moves across the day, a fixed food source can call for different waggle-run angles at different times. A dance therefore reflects the sun's position at the moment it is performed, so one site can be advertised with several angles.

Each waggle run is followed by a return loop that brings the dancer back to the start of the next run. The loop itself is not a second advertised destination, so the straight runs carry the directional information. A follower that tracks the sequence therefore attends to the runs, while the loops only organize the repetition of those runs.

Divergence among repeated runs measures variation around the advertised angle. A systematic bias in the average bearing is a different error, and the two have different consequences for a follower. An average bearing can be correct while individual runs vary widely, so the spread of runs and their mean angle answer separate questions. The mean angle gives the bearing, and the spread shows reliability.
notes: Waggle angles vary across repeated runs.

inserts.title: Displaced recruits keep the flight vector
paragraphs: The harmonic radar transponder marks where the bee is, not a neural signal, so each track is a record of position over time. Reading a recruit's flight therefore means reading its path through the landscape. Each track also begins at the point where the recruit was released, so the starting site is part of the record.

Search counts as a genuine part of recruitment rather than an error-free continuation of the initial vector. Its later phase therefore belongs to the navigation itself, not to noise in the endpoint data. Recruits that search follow a different routine from those flying straight, and both phases belong to the same recruitment event. Counting that phase keeps the full recruitment event in view.

Ground velocity combines the bee's movement through the air with air movement over the ground. Air drift can push the heading away from the destination direction, so heading and destination are different quantities. Measuring both allows the two to be told apart, and the difference between them is what the recruit corrects for. Both must be kept separate to read a track.
notes: Displaced recruits keep the flight vector.

The harmonic radar transponder marks where the bee is, not a neural signal, so each track is a record of position over time
Reading a recruit's flight therefore means reading its path through the landscape. Each track also begins at the point where the recruit was released, so the starting site is part of the record.

inserts.title: Tunnel texture drives the visual odometer
paragraphs: Waggle duration is the measured motor output of the dance. The texture contrast addresses distance estimation rather than reward quality, so a change in dance type reflects the visual input. Followers decode the dance, so the difference reaches them as a change in the message they receive. Reward quality was not the variable under test.

A tunnel flight is interpreted through the outdoor relation without being equated with an ordinary outdoor flight. The tunnel result is therefore a reading of the signal, not a claim about how far the bee flew outdoors. The dance itself is the only evidence that the reading uses, so the inference stays tied to the signal.

Stripes and random texture impose different visual motion while the target location stays the same. The dance type therefore reflects the visual input received along the route, with the physical destination held fixed. The texture comparison isolates visual input from reward and location within a single design. Sensory input is the only variable that changes.

inserts.title: Short tunnel journeys signal long distances
paragraphs: The tunnel results establish a visual dependence of the signal without requiring any claim that the bee perceived meters. The duration itself is a measured motor output, and the outdoor relation gives that output its distance reading. The signal therefore carries information about the visual route, not about the bee's sense of length. This keeps the interpretation on the signal side.

This relation is applied to the tunnel passages without treating them as ordinary outdoor flights. The reading therefore describes what the dance signals about the route, not a measured outdoor journey. The calibration itself was measured on outdoor feeders, so the tunnel values are set against an independent outdoor scale. Both arrangements sit on the same scale.

Two arrangements with different outdoor approach lengths produced readings that both exceed the physical journey. Their shared pattern points to the visual surroundings as the source of the inflated signal, consistent with the close textured walls both passages shared. Neither reading depends on the length actually flown outdoors, because both values come from the same calibration.
notes: Short tunnel journeys signal long distances.

inserts.title: Closing the tunnel stops recruitment
paragraphs: The dancer and the follower can share a visual interpretation because both navigate comparable terrain along the route. That shared terrain links the advertised tunnel distance to the search that follows. The tunnel distance is therefore decoded in visual terms rather than in meters. The link depends on the terrain both bees experience. Both bees use that terrain for orientation.

Bees arriving at the control stations were captured, so their own return dances could not add recruitment to a station. The search pattern therefore tests how followers decode a dance, independently of the dancer's physical flight length. Station arrivals measure the decoding alone, since the stations offered no reward. Recruitment therefore reflects the dance information alone.

The physical feeder distance and the searched distance are experimentally distinct quantities. Recruit searches measure the followers' interpretation of the dance, not the feeder's physical position. Each search site is therefore a readout of a visual calibration. The experiment reports searched distances in meters from the hive. Searches are reported as distances from the hive.
notes: Closing the tunnel stops recruitment.

inserts.title: Land scenes carry more image contrast
paragraphs: Low contrast can weaken motion signals even when the animal keeps moving. The water segments therefore reduce the effective image motion the odometer receives, even though the bee continues flying across them. The odometer's rate of accumulation is set by that input, so a slower rise in duration over water follows from the image structure.

The photographs document the actual terrain rather than a reconstructed visual stimulus. Their measurement windows therefore reflect the scene a bee flew over, which gives the contrast values a direct link to real foraging routes. Each photograph was taken along the route a recruit actually flew. Those windows were applied to every scene in the same way.

A correlation across route segments also tracks flight height, viewing direction and surface texture. Those factors vary together along a route, so contrast is one of several linked variables. The controlled tunnel-texture experiments supply a separate intervention on visual motion, which isolates one variable at a time. The tunnel manipulation alone changes texture while holding the rest of the route fixed.
notes: Land scenes carry more image contrast.

inserts.title: Tracing links the dorsal rim to the MEDRA
paragraphs: Sakura and colleagues repeated the polarization conditioning with ultraviolet, blue and green light. Bees learned the rewarded e-vector under ultraviolet light and not under blue or green light, so the learned response depends on which wavelengths reach the eye. The rewarded and unrewarded e-vectors were kept identical across all three conditions, so the spectral input was the sole difference between them.

A wavelength-independent task solution would have produced learning under all three colors. The failure under blue and green light therefore points to spectral sensitivity of the polarization input rather than to a harder task. Sucrose responsiveness was tested in a separate control, so reward strength is not the explanation. The spectral dependence is therefore a property of the learned response itself.

The ultraviolet dependence is a behavioral result, measured in trained bees across the three wavelength conditions. It identifies which part of the spectrum the learned polarization response requires, and it sets the wavelength range that any later test of the dorsal-rim pathway should use. This dependence points to a sensory input the pathway can use, and the next experiment in the sequence traces where that input goes.

inserts.title: Polarization axis sets the dance axis
paragraphs: The polarizer orientation changed while the tunnel direction stayed fixed, so the two groups differed only in the polarization pattern. Any difference between their dances therefore came from that pattern. Both groups flew the same textured tunnel, and their dances were measured on the comb after training. The diffuser was used in both groups, which holds the sky cue constant for both groups.

The original article provides the preparation images and the measured dance distributions. The direction plots in this deck were not reconstructed from raw data, so the reported axes are the authors' own values. The mean axes were measured separately for the transverse and axial groups. The authors' numbers are reported directly in the source. Both values come from that source.

The signal therefore carries an orientation on the comb, and the sign of the direction is missing. Each group's waggle runs came from the same comb and were measured the same way, so the two axes are directly comparable. Such a signal narrows the possible headings to one line on the comb. The axis carries the information the bees conveyed.

inserts.title: Cloud cover removes direct sun sight
paragraphs: The actual daily course of the sun was known independently from astronomical position. The bees' dances can therefore be judged by a reference calculated from astronomy. The two groups' dance orientations can then be checked against that reference across the test, which makes the astronomical course an independent standard. The astronomical course is the reference for the dances.

Direction in this experiment was inferred from dances relative to a known food route. No electrode recorded a sun representation in the bees, so the solar estimate comes from the dance orientation alone. The inference therefore rests on what the dancers communicated, not on neural recordings. Dance orientation is the only measured quantity in this comparison.

Shared cloud cover controlled the immediate celestial cues available to both groups. The remaining difference between the two dance patterns therefore reflects the bees' training history under matched sky conditions. Both groups were tested on the same cloudy day. The bees' flight histories were the factor that differed. Sky conditions were identical for both groups.
notes: Cloud cover removes direct sun sight.

inserts.title: Anesthesia delays the hive's activity rhythm
paragraphs: Cryptochrome and period expression were sampled across the daily cycle rather than at a single time after treatment. A sampling schedule of this kind shows the whole rhythm, not a snapshot of one moment in the day. Sampling across the day sets the timing of each measurement, so a phase shift can be seen directly.

A phase shift changes when the rhythm peaks, not simply whether a gene is expressed. A delay in the rhythm therefore appears as a change in timing, and expression levels can remain similar while their peaks move. Shifts in timing are the quantity that matters here, not the on-off state of each gene. Peak timing is what a phase shift moves.

Both the anesthetic target and the cells supplying timing to the compass pathway are left unidentified here. Averaging over whole brains hides which cells those are, so the mechanism stays open. This study measured the hive, not individual cells, and identifying the cells is required before the timing signal can be traced. The cells are the open question here.

inserts.title: PDF fibers lie beside transmedulla neurons
paragraphs: Immunoreactivity means that an antibody recognizes its target in the preparation. Staining establishes that the labeled substance is present in a region. A specific connection needs separate evidence, since a labeled structure is a location and not yet a connection. Its function needs a separate test, and staining alone gives that test no answer. The labels are therefore evidence of presence only.

Close proximity is a candidate contact. Peptide release, a postsynaptic PDF receptor and a functional synapse would each need separate evidence before any of them could be assumed to operate in this pathway. The two labels were also examined at higher magnification to measure that proximity. The two labels were combined in a single preparation.

A nearby labeled bouton marks a possible site of contact. Its role in circadian compass correction is a proposal drawn from how the two labels sit in the medulla. The contact therefore stays a candidate until other methods test it in this preparation. Its strength depends on the staining conditions used in that preparation. The labels were examined in one layer.
notes: PDF fibers lie beside transmedulla neurons.

inserts.title: Separated complexes lie in both bulbs
paragraphs: Electron microscopy showed that large TuLAL1 terminals contain vesicles and several presynaptic specializations, each facing smaller profiles. Vesicles are membrane-bound structures that store the signaling molecules a terminal releases onto the processes it contacts. In the electron images they appear as small membrane-bound profiles clustered at the presynaptic specialization.

A dyadic contact is one presynaptic specialization facing two postsynaptic profiles, and a tetradic contact is one facing four. Counting the profiles at each specialization describes the local arrangement of a contact, not the total number of targets a presynaptic neuron has.

GABA immunostaining associated the downstream TL neurons with an inhibitory transmitter phenotype. That staining makes inhibition a candidate component of the signaling at these contacts, alongside the excitatory input that the terminals convey. The staining identifies a transmitter class, a different measure from the contact geometry described in the first two paragraphs.

inserts.title: Learned field cues persist for 24 h
paragraphs: Treatments applied after conditioning distinguish sensory access at test from the initial acquisition of the association. Bees were first trained with their antennae intact, which sets the association before any manipulation. Learning is therefore held constant while the sensory access alone changes. Treatments at test then probe what the bees currently use. The timing of the treatment is the variable under study.

Coating the surfaces and restricting the joints are different manipulations, and they produced different reductions in the learned response. Each treatment targets a distinct route of mechanical input from the antenna. A coating that leaves the joints mobile is therefore a weaker manipulation of joint input than restriction. The two treatments are compared on the same learned response.

The conditioned response to electric cues was retained for 24 h after conditioning. Learning therefore persisted across a full day, which places the field cue within a memory that outlasts a single training session. The retention test was run on the same bees that had learned the cue, so the memory belongs to those individuals.
notes: Learned field cues persist for 24 h.

inserts.title: Mature foragers differ from young workers
paragraphs: Directional divergence measures variation among the waggle runs within a dance. It is a different quantity from a shift in the mean direction a dancer advertises, and the two kinds of error affect followers in different ways. Both measures come from the same set of recorded dances.

The two measures therefore separate two sources of imprecision. Spread across runs describes how consistently one dancer signals, while bias describes whether the average signal points in the correct direction. Each source of error is measured on its own, so a dancer's consistency and its accuracy are not confused.

A dance can therefore be precise without being accurate, or accurate without being precise. Identifying which error dominates shows whether a dance is noisy or systematically shifted, and the two readouts answer different questions about the same signal.
notes: Mature foragers differ from young workers.

Directional divergence measures variation among the waggle runs within a dance

It is a different quantity from a shift in the mean direction a dancer advertises, and the two kinds of error affect followers in different ways. Both measures come from the same set of recorded dances.

2: **Waggle dances** are repeated movements on the vertical comb that tell nestmates where a food source lies. Each dance contains a straight abdominal-wagging run and alternating return loops. A **vector** specifies a direction and a distance from an origin, and for a forager's dance that origin is the hive. The dance takes place inside the hive.

Dong and colleagues recorded marked foragers that visited a feeder 150 m from the hive. On the vertical comb, the angle of the waggle run encoded the food's direction relative to the sun, and the run's duration encoded its distance. Followers stayed close to the dancer and attended to every run. Marked bees made each visit traceable.

The signal describes a place outside the hive rather than the dancer's immediate position. Video recordings measure the spatial and temporal structure of the message. Successful communication also requires that followers pick up the signal and then choose an appropriate flight. Dance followers can therefore act on information about a place they have not visited.
3: A dancer on a vertical comb treats upward as the sun's direction. The waggle-run angle measured from vertical stands for the resource's direction relative to the sun outside, so **gravity** substitutes for the sun in a dark hive. The message carries a direction even where no sunlight reaches the dancer. This shared reference works in darkness.

Dong and colleagues recorded dance angles on the crowded, uneven comb surface. Repeated waggle runs spread around a mean angle, so the team measured that **divergence** rather than assuming each run conveyed an identical angle. Bees without experienced dancers produced the largest spread in their first dances. Divergence in direction is therefore a measure of precision.

Encoding direction involves a reference system and motor precision in executing the angle. A follower must convert the comb-relative angle into a flight direction using celestial information. The dancer's output supplies the first half of that conversion, which is why the recordings measure precision as well as direction. Angle precision and direction are both measured.
4: Von Frisch and Lindauer trained marked foragers to a feeder 180 m away, in a direction 30° north of west from the hive. The bees learned this route during the afternoon. The team then moved the hive into an unfamiliar landscape to test the learned bearing. The sun's position changed between afternoon training and morning flight.

The following morning, equally familiar scented food dishes were offered in four directions in the new landscape. Arriving bees were captured at once, so successful visitors could not return and recruit nestmates. Searches favored the trained **compass direction** despite the changed surroundings. Each dish carried the same familiar scent, so the choices reflect the bees' learned bearing.

The result points to compensation for the sun's movement between afternoon training and morning flight. In related tests, cloudy skies prevented correct orientation when neither direct sunlight nor polarized skylight was available. Landmarks and celestial cues can compete with each other during orientation. Some cues compete, so orientation depends on which information is available.
5: Riley and colleagues tracked bees that had followed dances advertising an unscented feeder 200 m east of the hive. A harmonic radar detects a small transponder carried by each bee, so the trajectory can be recorded outside the observation hive. Positions were sampled every 3 s. Recording outside the hive makes the whole flight measurable.

Recruits released at the hive generally flew an initially straight eastward route. Their straight sections averaged 206 m before searching began. Radar positions allowed **directed travel** to be told apart from more tortuous search behavior. The straight flight came first, and searching followed it in most tracks, so the radar records two distinct phases of each recruit's flight.

The recruits had never visited the advertised feeder, and the unscented food and wind direction reduced direct odor guidance from the destination. The flight therefore reflects a **flight vector** acquired from the dance. Radar records the flight itself, while the sensory cues a follower used during the dance remain unmeasured. The flight vector therefore reflects what the dance told them.
6: Riley and colleagues captured dance followers at the hive and released them 200–250 m southwest of it. This manipulation kept the dance's instruction unchanged while moving the starting point. From the release site, the feeder lay in a new direction and at a new distance. The flight began from an origin the dance did not specify.

Rather than redirecting toward the feeder from the release point, displaced bees began with an eastward straight flight that averaged 188 m before search.
